title: Quadratic formula & discriminant
examples: When should I use the quadratic formula instead of factoring?
What does a negative discriminant mean for my graph?
Can you show me the derivation of the formula again?

explain.say: Today we learn about the quadratic formula and the discriminant. This helps us solve any quadratic equation. A quadratic equation looks like this: a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero.

The formula is derived by completing the square on the general form. This process gives us the general solution for x. The formula is x equals negative b plus or minus the square root of b squared minus four a c, all divided by two a.

items: Start with general form: ax² + bx + c = 0
Complete the square on the general form
Derive the general solution for x

explain.say: The part under the square root is called the discriminant. We write it as the capital letter delta. The discriminant is b squared minus four a c. This value tells us about the type of solutions we will find.
If the discriminant is greater than zero, there are two distinct real solutions. If it equals zero, there is exactly one real solution. If it is less than zero, there are no real solutions.

draw.text: Δ > 0: Two real roots; Δ = 0: One real root; Δ < 0: No real roots

explain.say: Sometimes we need exact answers, leaving the square root as is. Other times, we must round the answer to a specific number of decimal places. Always check the question for rounding instructions.

faq.q: What is the discriminant actually telling me?
faq.a: The discriminant tells you about the nature of the roots of the equation. It tells you how many times the graph crosses the x-axis.
asks: How do I know if there are real solutions?
What does the value of b squared minus four a c mean?

faq.q: If the discriminant is negative, does that mean I made a mistake?
faq.a: No, it just means the solutions are not real numbers. They are complex numbers, which is a different topic.
asks: Can I solve it if delta is negative?
What kind of roots are they then?

faq.q: Do I always have to use the quadratic formula?
faq.a: No, if you can factor the equation easily, factoring is much faster. Use the formula when factoring is difficult or impossible.
asks: Is there an easier way than the formula?
When is factoring better than the formula?

faq.q: When should I provide an exact answer versus a rounded one?
faq.a: Always follow the instructions given in the question. If it asks for exact, leave the root symbol. If it asks for decimal places, round carefully.
asks: How do I know if I need to round?
What is the difference between exact and decimal answers?

faq.q: What are a, b, and c in the equation?
faq.a: These are the coefficients of the quadratic equation. They are the numbers multiplying x squared, x, and the constant term respectively.
asks: Where do I find a, b, and c?
What do the letters a, b, and c stand for?

facts: A quadratic equation has the general form a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero.
The quadratic formula is x equals negative b plus or minus the square root of b squared minus four a c, all divided by two a.
If the discriminant is zero, the quadratic equation has exactly one real solution, also called a repeated root.
When rounding, always check the required number of decimal places specified in the problem.

quiz.say: Solve x squared plus 5 x plus 6 equals zero.
quiz.why: This equation can be factored easily into (x plus 2)(x plus 3) equals zero, giving the solutions x equals negative two and x equals negative three.

wrong.1: This is a common mistake from incorrectly adding the coefficients.
wrong.2: This mistake happens when students forget to account for the negative signs in the factors.
wrong.3: This incorrectly assumes the constant term must be zero.

quiz.say: What is the value of the discriminant for three x squared minus two x plus one equals zero?
quiz.why: Here, a is three, b is negative two, and c is one. The calculation is negative two squared minus four times three times one, which equals negative one.

wrong.0: This calculation incorrectly uses the value of c instead of multiplying it by four.
wrong.2: This results from incorrectly calculating b squared as two instead of four.
wrong.3: This mistake occurs when the student forgets to multiply the four by the coefficient a.

quiz.say: Find the value of k so that x squared plus 4 x plus k equals zero has exactly one real solution.
quiz.why: For one real solution, the discriminant must be zero. Using a is one, b is four, and c is k, we get four squared minus four times one times k equals zero, so 16 minus 4k equals zero, meaning k equals four.

wrong.0: This suggests the student subtracted the terms incorrectly.
wrong.1: This is a common guess when students think the constant term must be zero.
wrong.3: This happens if the student incorrectly sets four squared equal to zero.
